## My request for Codex:
how do i make pvpython and vtkmodules available in the disperse conda environment permanently? can i set any paths that stay set between sessions?

<a id="t-000656"></a>
### 2026-01-01 22:53:03Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0239)

Two reliable ways:

1) Install VTK into the env (preferred if versions match your ParaView):
```bash
conda activate disperse
conda install -c conda-forge vtk  # picks version compatible with your Python
```
Then just run `python scripts/analyze_snapshot.py ...`; no extra PATH/PYTHONPATH needed.

2) Reuse ParaView’s Python runtime permanently:
- Add ParaView’s bin and Python libs to the env’s activate hook so they’re set on every `conda activate disperse`.
Create the files (paths adapted to your system/Python version):
```
mkdir -p $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d

cat > $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d/paraview_path.sh <<'EOF'
export _PV_OLD_PATH="$PATH"
export _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH="$PYTHONPATH"
export PATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin:$PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python:${PYTHONPATH}"
EOF

cat > $CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d/paraview_path.sh <<'EOF'
export PATH="$_PV_OLD_PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="$_PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH"
unset _PV_OLD_PATH _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH
EOF
```
- Reactivate the env (`conda deactivate && conda activate disperse`). Now `pvpython` and `vtkmodules` are on PATH/PYTHONPATH every session.

Pick one approach; don’t mix. If you go with the hook, ensure the ParaView Python path matches your install (check `/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python`).

## My request for Codex:
I want to simplify how I call pvpython, so instead of prepending it with the path, i would prefer to automat this by activating the conda environment. how do i do that?

<a id="t-000664"></a>
### 2026-01-01 23:06:35Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0247)

You can make `pvpython` available automatically whenever you `conda activate disperse` by putting ParaView’s bin on PATH inside the env’s activate hook (and restoring on deactivate). You already created the hook; just ensure it contains the ParaView bin and standard paths, e.g.:

```bash
mkdir -p "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d" "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d"

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'
export _PV_OLD_PATH="$PATH"
export _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH="$PYTHONPATH"
export PATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:$PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="/Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/Python:${PYTHONPATH}"
EOF

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'
export PATH="$_PV_OLD_PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="$_PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH"
unset _PV_OLD_PATH _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH
EOF
```

Then reactivate the env:

```bash
conda deactivate
conda activate disperse
```

After that, you can just run:

```bash
pvpython scripts/batch_clip.py ...your args...
```

No path prefix needed. If you prefer, you can instead symlink pvpython into the env’s `bin`:

```bash
ln -s /Applications/ParaView-6.0.1.app/Contents/bin/pvpython "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/pvpython"
```

Either approach makes `pvpython` available whenever the env is active.

Looks like your current shell PATH inside the env is missing `/bin` and `/usr/bin`, so even `mkdir`/`cat` aren’t found. First restore the standard system paths, then create the hook files:

```bash
# Temporarily restore standard system paths in this shell

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/activate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'

cat > "$CONDA_PREFIX/etc/conda/deactivate.d/paraview_path.sh" <<'EOF'
export PATH="$_PV_OLD_PATH"
export PYTHONPATH="$_PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH"
unset _PV_OLD_PATH _PV_OLD_PYTHONPATH
EOF
```

Then reactivate to apply:

```bash
conda deactivate
conda activate disperse
```

After that, `pvpython` should be on PATH automatically.

Otherwise the command you posted is fine; just ensure VTK is importable in that session.

### 2026-01-01 23:33:03Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0264)

Key points:

- `PYTHONPATH="" python …` strips ParaView’s libs, so unless VTK is installed in your conda env, the stats code can’t read VTU/VTP and no CSV is written.
- `batch_clip.py` already works via `pvpython`; it does not need `PYTHONPATH` set to ParaView—`pvpython` bundles its own modules.

Safe path forward (won’t break `batch_clip.py`):

1) Remove the ParaView `PYTHONPATH` export from your conda hooks (keep PATH if you like, but drop PYTHONPATH to avoid the NumPy mismatch). Then `conda deactivate && conda activate disperse` so PYTHONPATH is empty.
2) Install VTK (and hdf5plugin) into the env so `python` can import them:
   ```
   conda install -c conda-forge vtk hdf5plugin
   ```
3) Verify:
   ```
   python - <<'PY'
   from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
   from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
   import numpy
   print("vtk stats stack ok")
   PY
   ```
4) Re-run your analyze command normally (no PYTHONPATH override). With VTK present and VTU/VTP outputs produced, `<prefix>_summary_stats.csv` will be written.

`batch_clip.py` remains fine: just call `pvpython scripts/batch_clip.py ...`; it uses its own VTK regardless of PYTHONPATH.

This will stop the VTK reader error and ensure the stats CSV uses the real file.

`netconv` itself appends the smoothing tag as `.S020` (or similar), so we don’t control that suffix. Renaming it to `_S020` isn’t an option without post-processing the files, and reverting the fallback would bring back the “file not found” error. The current glob-based detection is the safe way to locate whatever filename `netconv` actually writes. I recommend keeping it.

For terminal usage, nothing new needs to go into the guides, but here’s the clean way to run both scripts:

- `analyze_snapshot.py` (using your conda env’s Python with its own VTK installed):
  ```
  python scripts/analyze_snapshot.py \
    --input data/snap_010.hdf5 \
    --output-dir outputs/snap_010_subbox \
    --crop-box 0 0 0 500000 500000 100000 \
    --stride 1 \
    --delaunay-btype periodic \
    --export-delaunay \
    --mse-nsig 3.0 \
    --dump-manifolds JE1a \
    --dump-arcs U \
    --netconv-smooth 20 \
    --skelconv-smooth 20
  ```
  (No trailing spaces after the `\`; keep `PYTHONPATH` empty so it uses the env’s NumPy/VTK.)

- `batch_clip.py` (use ParaView’s interpreter):
  ```
  pvpython scripts/batch_clip.py \
    --input-dir outputs/snap_010_cropped \
    --walls snap_010_manifolds_vtu_JE1a.S020.vtu \
    --filaments snap_010_filaments_U_vtp.S020.vtp \
    --delaunay snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu \
    --output-dir outputs/snap_010_cropped/auto2d \
    --output-prefix snap_010 \
    --slab-axis z --slab-origin 0 --slab-thickness 10 \
    --resample-dims 512 512 64 \
    --scalar-name log_field_value \
    --save-pngs
  ```

If you add ParaView’s bin to PATH via the conda activate hook, you can omit the full path and just call `pvpython …`.

  - Loops over non-overlapping crop boxes (default 500×500×100 Mpc/h within 0–1000 ranges).
  - Runs `analyze_snapshot.py` for each crop (keeps crop info in folder/prefix names).
  - Then, for each crop, runs `batch_clip.py` over slab origins stepped in 10 Mpc (default), writing results to slab-specific subfolders.
  - Names include crop tags and slab origins to keep outputs organized.
  - Uses smoothing suffixes when building expected filenames (e.g., `.S020` when smoothing >0).

Usage example (adjust as needed):
```bash
python scripts/batch_crop_and_clip.py \
  --snapshot data/snap_010.hdf5 \
  --output-root outputs/quijote_batches \
  --crop-size 500 500 100 \
  --x-range 0 1000 --y-range 0 1000 --z-range 0 1000 \
  --slab-step 10 --slab-thickness 10 \
  --dump-manifolds JE1a --dump-arcs U \
  --netconv-smooth 20 --skelconv-smooth 20 \
  --resample-dims 512 512 64 \
  --scalar-name log_field_value
```

Notes:
- It calls `analyze_snapshot.py` with your current Python; ensure VTK/hdf5plugin are available there.
- It calls `pvpython` for `batch_clip.py`; make sure `pvpython` is on PATH.
- Smoothing tags are assumed to follow `.S###` (e.g., `.S020`); adjust smoothing args to match your netconv/skelconv settings.

In this pipeline the units do matter:

- `analyze_snapshot.py` expects `--crop-box` in the snapshot’s input units (default `kpc/h`). It then rescales all coordinates to the output unit (default `mpc/h`) before writing VTU/VTP.
- The `batch_crop_and_clip.py` ranges (`--x-range`, `--y-range`, `--z-range`, `--crop-size`) are passed straight into `--crop-box`, so they must be in the snapshot’s input units (kpc/h unless you override `--input-unit`).
- `batch_clip.py` operates on the VTU/VTP outputs, which are in the **output** units from `analyze_snapshot` (mpc/h by default), so `--slab-origin`, `--slab-thickness`, and `--slab-step` should be in mpc/h if you use the defaults.

So in your test run with `--x-range 0 500` etc., you were defining 500 kpc/h boxes (~0.5 Mpc/h), which likely contained no particles. To cover 500 Mpc/h spans, either:

- Provide ranges/crop sizes in kpc/h: e.g. `--crop-size 500000 500000 100000` and matching ranges, or
- Set both units to mpc/h when running analyze: `--input-unit mpc/h --output-unit mpc/h`, then keep ranges/crop sizes in mpc/h.

Likewise, set slab step/thickness in the same units as the VTU/VTP (mpc/h if you keep the default output unit).

### 2026-01-02 04:55:03Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0284)

`batch_clip.py` itself doesn’t enforce “stay within the crop” beyond using whatever bounds it’s given: it computes `slab_bounds = _compute_bounds(reader.GetDataInformation(), axis, z0, thick)` and then clips. If `z0/thickness` extend outside the dataset’s bounds, the extraction can come back empty (and downstream code will error, e.g., `GetPoints()` returning `None`). There’s no internal clamp.

The safer layer is the driver (`batch_crop_and_clip.py`), which now:
- Derives the slab range from the crop’s z-extent and converts to the output units, and
- Breaks out of the slab loop when `slab_origin + slab_thickness` would exceed that extent.

So as long as you keep slab origins/thickness within the crop’s z-range (in the output units of the VTU/VTP), the slabs won’t overrun. If you run `batch_clip.py` directly, you still need to ensure `--slab-origin`/`--slab-thickness` fit inside the dataset bounds.

- Read wall VTU and filament VTP.

Here’s a concrete, ID-based approach you can run in Python to get overlaps and mass/density by topology:

1) Read the meshes (walls VTU, filaments VTP) with VTK’s Python bindings:
   ```python
   from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
   from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa

   def read_vtk(path):
       if path.endswith(".vtu"):
           r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader()
       else:
           r = vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
       r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
       return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())
   walls = read_vtk("…_manifolds_vtu_….vtu")
   fils  = read_vtk("…_filaments_….vtp")
   ```

2) Pick a stable ID to join on (e.g., `true_index` or `source_index`). Extract as numpy arrays:
   ```python
   wall_ids = set(map(int, walls.PointData["true_index"]))
   fil_ids  = set(map(int, fils.PointData["true_index"]))
   shared   = wall_ids & fil_ids
   only_wall = wall_ids - fil_ids
   only_fil  = fil_ids - wall_ids
   ```

3) Build masks for each category:
   ```python
   import numpy as np
   w_ids = np.asarray(walls.PointData["true_index"], int)
   f_ids = np.asarray(fils.PointData["true_index"], int)
   mask_shared_w  = np.isin(w_ids, list(shared))
   mask_only_w    = np.isin(w_ids, list(only_wall))
   mask_shared_f  = np.isin(f_ids, list(shared))
   mask_only_f    = np.isin(f_ids, list(only_fil))
   ```

4) Sum/average the scalars you care about (e.g., `mass`, `field_value`, `log_field_value`) with those masks:
   ```python
   def stats(vals, mask):
       sel = vals[mask]
       return {"count": sel.size, "sum": float(sel.sum()), "mean": float(sel.mean()) if sel.size else 0.0}
   wall_mass = np.asarray(walls.PointData["mass"])
   fil_mass  = np.asarray(fils.PointData["mass"])
   print("shared mass (walls points that are shared):", stats(wall_mass, mask_shared_w))
   print("only-wall mass:", stats(wall_mass, mask_only_w))
   print("shared mass (fil points that are shared):", stats(fil_mass, mask_shared_f))
   print("only-fil mass:", stats(fil_mass, mask_only_f))
   # Repeat for density arrays as needed.
   ```

5) If you prefer to aggregate per critical point, loop over the unique IDs and sum the scalar values for each ID (e.g., use `np.bincount` with an index mapping).

Notes:
- Use the ID array that survives your netconv/skelconv (check for `true_index`, `source_index`, or `index` in the point data).
- Smoothing moves coordinates but keeps IDs, so the ID join is more reliable than geometric proximity.
- If you want spatial overlap instead, you’d need a spatial join (e.g., nearest-neighbor) between point clouds, but the ID approach above directly tells you shared vs unique and lets you sum mass/density for each set.

In DisPerSE outputs those three fields serve different bookkeeping roles:

- `index`: the vertex/cell ID in the current mesh as written by that run (after any masking, gathering, smoothing). It’s the local ID for this file.
- `true_index`: the original ID of that vertex in the NDnet before any gather/relabeling; use this to match across files from the same run even if they were smoothed or converted.
- `source_index`: links back to the critical point(s) or Delaunay element that generated the object. For manifolds you may see multiple `source_index` components (e.g., per dimension), pointing to the critical points that define that surface. For skeletons, it’s typically the critical point ID associated with the node/arc.

For reconciling walls/filaments, match on `true_index` (or `source_index` if you’re explicitly following the critical-point lineage); `index` alone can change between converted/smoothed files.

Doing it directly from the MSE outputs is possible, but it requires parsing the native formats. Here’s how I’d approach it and what “points not in either” would mean:

- **What’s in the native files:**
  - `*.NDnet` (manifolds/walls) contains critical points (0-cells) plus many non-critical vertices from the surface triangulation, with fields like `index/true_index/source_index` and scalars.
  - `*.NDskl` (filaments) stores the skeleton nodes (critical points) and arcs; endpoints carry the same IDs (`true_index/source_index`).

- **Overlap/unique via native IDs:**
  - Extract `true_index` (or `source_index`) from NDskl nodes and NDnet vertices.
  - Intersect for shared critical points; differences for unique-to-walls/unique-to-filaments.
  - “Points not in either” would be anything in the NDnet that is not tagged to a filament (if you treat NDnet vertices as the universe), or all critical points in the MSC minus those tagged to walls/filaments. If you instead mean particles outside any topology, you’d need the NDfield/NDnet vertices that are not in either structure.

- **Practical parsing options:**
  - Easiest: convert to ASCII once (`netconv -to ndnet_ascii` and `skelconv -to ndskl_ascii`, no smoothing) and parse those text files in Python. That preserves IDs and scalars without adding smoothing/resampling artifacts.
  - Or, keep using VTU/VTP but set smoothing to 0 to avoid resampling, ensuring ID/scalar arrays survive conversion, and compute overlaps there.

- **Script outline for native ASCII:**
  1) Convert walls to `ndnet_ascii` and filaments to `ndskl_ascii` (no smoothing).
  2) Write a small Python helper to read those text files, pull `true_index` (and `mass/field_value` if present), compute sets (shared/unique/none), and sum/average the scalar arrays per category. If you also want “not in either,” define your universe (all NDnet vertices or all critical points from the MSC) and subtract the wall/filament sets.

If you want, I can add a helper script that parses the ASCII NDnet/NDskl outputs, computes shared/unique/none counts and mass/density aggregates, and writes a CSV. That keeps `analyze_snapshot.py` untouched and avoids smoothing-induced data loss.

### 2026-01-02 21:13:06Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

There is a “universe” NDnet: the Delaunay NDnet written right after `delaunay_3D` contains all vertices/cells of the tessellation, with `field_value/log_field_value/mass` arrays. You can use it as the superset, but with a couple of caveats:

- Filaments: NDskl nodes are a subset of the critical points from the NDnet/MS complex. Their `true_index`/`source_index` IDs map back to the Delaunay NDnet.
- Walls: the manifold NDnet (and its VTU) contains critical points plus many additional vertices created by intersecting/sampling the surface. Only the critical-point vertices share IDs with the Delaunay NDnet; the extra surface vertices won’t match anything in the original NDnet.
- Delaunay NDnet vertex IDs aren’t 1:1 with particles; they’re the vertices of the tessellation. If you truly want “particles not in any topology,” you’d need to go back to the NDfield/particle list and classify, but that’s a different problem.

So you can approximate “not in either topology” as:

1) Convert the Delaunay NDnet to `ndnet_ascii` (no smoothing), collect its `true_index` as the universe.
2) Collect `true_index` from the filament NDskl (critical points) and from the manifold NDnet (only the IDs that exist; ignore the added surface vertices).
3) Universe minus (walls ∪ filaments) gives you NDnet vertices not attached to either topology. Mass/density can be summed from the Delaunay NDnet arrays for those IDs.

This works as long as you:
- Keep smoothing off when you need ID fidelity, and
- Accept that wall surface vertices beyond the critical points won’t appear in the universe set (they don’t reduce the “not in either” count).

If you want me to script this, I’ll base it on the Delaunay NDnet + manifold NDnet + NDskl ASCII files and output a CSV with shared/unique/unassigned counts and mass/density sums.

Mostly yes, with a few nuances:

- Filaments (NDskl): The node IDs (`true_index`/`source_index`) map back to the Delaunay NDnet vertices, so you can sum the DTFE `mass/field_value` on those IDs directly in the Delaunay NDnet.

- Walls (manifold NDnet): The critical-point vertices (0-cells) carry the same IDs and map back cleanly. The many extra surface vertices generated when triangulating/smoothing the manifold do not have a 1:1 counterpart in the Delaunay NDnet. If you stick to the critical IDs (and any `source_index` fields) you can attribute mass back to the original NDnet; if you try to include every surface vertex, many won’t match the Delaunay vertex list.

- Universe coverage: With stride = 1 inside a crop, the Delaunay NDnet contains one vertex per particle in that crop. Summing `mass` (or `field_value`) over a set of Delaunay vertex IDs tells you the total for those particles. “Unassigned” mass = all Delaunay IDs minus the union of the filament and wall critical IDs.

So yes: use the Delaunay NDnet as the universe, map filament and wall critical IDs back via `true_index`/`source_index`, and sum the Delaunay scalars over those IDs to get mass/density per topology. Just don’t expect every wall surface vertex to map; rely on the critical IDs for a consistent join.

- Yes, manifolds and skeletons have extra vertices beyond the critical points. They’re created where the manifold cuts the Delaunay cells or where arcs are resampled/smoothed—mainly for geometry. They typically carry interpolated scalars (density, etc.), but they don’t have a one-to-one origin in the Delaunay NDnet, so you can’t cleanly “trace” them back to a single Delaunay vertex.

- Mass attribution is safest via the Delaunay vertex IDs, not the interpolated manifold/skeleton vertices. Use the critical-point IDs that survive (`true_index` or `source_index`) to map back to the Delaunay NDnet and sum its `mass`/`field_value` there. Ignore the extra interpolated vertices for accounting.

- `true_index` is unique per vertex and is usually the best join key back to the Delaunay NDnet. `source_index` can be multi-component (e.g., multiple defining criticals), so it’s less convenient for a direct one-to-one join.

`ndtopo_stats.py` expects the ASCII variants. The simplest path is to convert your existing native files once, then point the helper at those:

- Delaunay NDnet → ASCII:
  ```
  netconv <path/to/delaunay.NDnet> -outName delaunay_ascii -outDir <out_dir> -to ndnet_ascii
  ```
- Manifolds NDnet → ASCII (use the same smoothing you already used, or none):
  ```
  netconv <path/to/manifolds.NDnet> -outName manifolds_ascii -outDir <out_dir> -to ndnet_ascii
  ```
- Skeleton NDskl → ASCII:
  ```
  skelconv <path/to/filaments.NDskl> -outName filaments_ascii -outDir <out_dir> -to ndskl_ascii
  ```

Then run:
```
python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py \
  --delaunay-ndnet <out_dir>/delaunay_ascii.NDnet \
  --walls-ndnet    <out_dir>/manifolds_ascii.NDnet \
  --filaments-ndskl <out_dir>/filaments_ascii.NDskl \
  --output-csv <out_dir>/topology_stats.csv
```

If you prefer, I can update `ndtopo_stats.py` to detect native NDnet/NDskl and spawn `netconv`/`skelconv` to ASCII on the fly, but the one-time conversion above is the most straightforward.

### 2026-01-02 23:19:28Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0342)

In the DisPerSE I/O conventions, the `cell` field on the skeleton references the originating NDnet cell. For 0‑cells, the integer part of `cell` is the NDnet vertex ID; the decimal part encodes the cell’s dimension/type. So if you need to map a 0‑cell back to the NDnet, use the integer part of `cell`—it’s the same identifier as the NDnet vertex ID (what the ASCII exports label as `true_index` for vertices).

### 2026-01-02 23:21:40Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0344)

For 0‑cells, yes: the `cell` field in the NDskl has a “N.dim” encoding where the integer part is the NDnet simplex ID and the decimal part encodes the dimension (0 for a vertex, 1 for an edge, etc.). A 0‑cell will have a `.0` decimal, so `int(cell)` gives you the NDnet vertex ID; that’s the same ID that appears as `true_index` on the NDnet vertices. So to join skeleton 0‑cells back to the NDnet, using `int(cell)` (or `true_index` if it’s present in the NDskl) is the right approach.

Caveats:
- Only 0‑cells will have `.0`; higher‑index critical points will have `.1/.2/.3` in `cell` because they sit on edges/faces/tets.
- If you’ve smoothed/resampled, stick to the native ASCII exports for fidelity.

The zeroed CSV comes from missing/empty IDs: in your run, the script reports `universe ids: 0, wall ids: 0, filament ids: 140527`, so there was nothing to match for Delaunay/walls.

Two likely causes:
- No VTK available in the current shell, so VTK fallback didn’t run. Ensure `vtkmodules` is importable (e.g., run `python - <<'PY'\nimport vtkmodules; print('vtk ok')\nPY` in the same shell). If that fails, install VTK in the env or use `pvpython`.
- The ID array name in your VTK files isn’t `true_index`. You may need to use another array (e.g., `index`, `source_index`, or `cell`).

What to do:
1) Make sure `vtkmodules` is available in the env you run `ndtopo_stats.py`. If not, install it (`conda install -c conda-forge vtk`) or run with `pvpython`.
2) Inspect the point-data arrays in your VTU/VTP to pick the right ID field. For example:
   ```bash
   python - <<'PY'
   from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
   from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
   files = ["outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu",
            "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_manifolds_vtu_JE1a.S020.vtu",
            "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_filaments_U_vtp.S020.vtp"]
   for f in files:
       r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if f.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
       r.SetFileName(f); r.Update()
       dobj = dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())
       print(f, list(dobj.PointData.keys()))
   PY
   ```
3) Re-run `ndtopo_stats.py` pointing to the VTK files and the correct ID arrays, e.g.:
   ```bash
   python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py --verbose \
     --delaunay-vtk outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu \
     --walls-vtk outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_manifolds_vtu_JE1a.S020.vtu \
     --filaments-vtk outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_filaments_U_vtp.S020.vtp \
     --walls-id-field index --filaments-id-field cell \
     --output-csv outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/topology_stats.csv
   ```
The script will try the given ID field and fall back to common alternatives (`true_index/index/source_index/cell`). Once it finds real IDs and VTK is available, you’ll get nonzero counts and sums.

- It now treats `.vtu/.vtp` inputs as VTK only (skips ASCII parsing), and you can rely solely on VTK files without decode errors.
- Added optional VTK args but made the required NDnet/NDSkl args tolerant of VTK files; ASCII parsing is skipped when the suffix isn’t `.NDnet`/`.NDskl`.
- Added ID-loading fallback and a final error if IDs couldn’t be loaded.
- Filament IDs now default to `cell` and take the integer part when parsing NDskl.

Please rerun with your VTK files only:

### 2026-01-03 02:03:51Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0373)

- **What it does now:** It reads the IDs and scalar arrays from the VTK files you point it at (`snap_010_delaunay_vtu.vtu`, `...manifolds...vtu`, `...filaments...vtp`). It uses the ID field you specify for walls (here `true_index`) and for filaments (`cell`, taking the integer part). It then computes the sets:
  - shared = walls ∩ filaments
  - wall_only = walls \ filaments
  - filament_only = filaments \ walls
  - unassigned = all Delaunay IDs \ (walls ∪ filaments)
  
  It aggregates counts and sums/means of the scalar fields you ask for (here `field_value` and `log_field_value`) using the values attached to those IDs in the Delaunay file. It writes those stats to the CSV.

- **Geometry distortion:** The VTU/VTP files can have smoothed/resampled geometry compared to native NDnet/NDskl, but the ID arrays (`true_index`, `cell`, etc.) carry over. We’re matching by ID, not by geometry, so the smoothing doesn’t affect the join.

- **ID matching:** Yes, it matches point IDs between walls/filaments and the Delaunay set. It uses the walls ID field you supply, the filament ID field you supply (integer part if `cell`), and uses the Delaunay IDs as the universe.

- **Which file supplies the scalar values:** The sums/means come from the Delaunay file for any IDs present there. The script currently pulls scalar arrays from the Delaunay input; the walls/filament inputs are only used for their ID sets. That assumes the same ID has consistent scalars across files; using the Delaunay scalars avoids any loss from netconv/skelconv. If you want to include `mass`, add it to `--scalar-fields mass field_value log_field_value`.

- **Consistency of scalar values:** For a given ID, the scalar values should match across outputs if the tools preserved them. By using the Delaunay file as the authoritative source, we avoid discrepancies. If you prefer to source scalars from walls/filaments instead, we can add that option, but the Delaunay file is the safest.

To include mass in the CSV, rerun with `--scalar-fields mass field_value log_field_value`; the script will sum/mean the `mass` values from the Delaunay file over each category.

```bash
}

wall_ids = set(map(int, ids["walls"]))

        fv = d["filaments"].PointData[field][fi] if field in d["filaments"].PointData.keys() else None
        print(f"ID {cid} {field}: delaunay={dv}, walls={wv}, filaments={fv}")
PY
```

<a id="t-000794"></a>
### 2026-01-03 02:48:44Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0377)

The mismatches are expected given how the scalars are produced:

- The Delaunay file’s `field_value/log_field_value` are the DTFE values on the Delaunay vertices. Those are the “raw” per-vertex scalars from your sampled particle set.
- The skeleton and manifold outputs are derived objects: MSE picks critical points, then netconv/skelconv can resample and smooth geometry and data. With `-smooth 20`, both geometry and point data are Laplacian-smoothed/interpolated, so the numbers no longer equal the original DTFE values at the same ID. Walls also include many non‑critical vertices where the scalar is interpolated along the surface.
- Even at critical points, the `field_value` stored in the NDskl/NDnet is the value at that critical cell (min/saddle/max), which isn’t guaranteed to equal the DTFE at the original Delaunay vertex once you’ve smoothed or after persistence simplification.

If you need scalars to match exactly by ID, re-export without smoothing (`-smooth 0` in netconv/skelconv) and use the native NDnet/NDskl ASCII; otherwise, treat the Delaunay values as authoritative for mass/density and use IDs only for overlap bookkeeping, since the wall/filament scalars may be interpolated or smoothed.

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0378)

<a id="t-000796"></a>
### 2026-01-03 02:51:24Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0379)

`field_value` and `log_field_value` are stored as separate arrays; the conversion/smoothing steps don’t guarantee one is the exact log of the other. In practice:

- `netconv`/`skelconv` interpolate/smooth point data; the smoothing can be applied independently to each array, so even if `field_value` happens to match for an ID, the stored `log_field_value` may be the smoothed/interpolated log from a different step.
- Some pipelines write `log_field_value` from the native NDnet/NDskl critical values, while `field_value` has been resampled, so they’re no longer in lockstep.
- Base/clamping can differ between the two arrays if they were generated separately.

If you need consistent pairs, pick one authoritative scalar (e.g., the Delaunay `field_value`), and compute its log yourself in post-processing. For exact matching across files, export without smoothing (`-smooth 0`) and/or recompute `log_field_value` from your chosen `field_value` rather than trusting both arrays to align.

We moved to VTK because the ASCII parsing kept failing (encoding errors, missing IDs) and VTK files are easier to read. However, you’re right: for sanity checks and unsmoothed values, the native NDnet/NDskl are better.

To sanity-check consistency without smoothing:

1) Use the native NDnet/NDskl and convert to ASCII without smoothing:
   ```
   netconv snap_010.NDnet -outName snap_010_ascii -outDir ... -to NDnet_ascii -smooth 0
   netconv snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a.NDnet -outName ... -to NDnet_ascii -smooth 0
   skelconv snap_010_s3.U.NDskl -outName ... -to NDskl_ascii -smooth 0
   ```

2) Run `ndtopo_stats.py` on those ASCII files with matching ID fields (e.g., `--walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell`) and check sums/means; the `field_value/log_field_value` should align because no smoothing/interpolation was applied.

3) If you still prefer VTK, re-export with `-smooth 0` for netconv/skelconv so the VTK arrays are the raw critical values.

In short: the switch to VTK was for convenience, but for exact scalar matching you should use the unsmoothed native (or unsmoothed VTK) outputs and confirm with a quick spot check.

Yes. Convert the native files to ASCII with no smoothing, then point `ndtopo_stats.py` at those ASCII files:

```bash
netconv snap_010.NDnet -outName snap_010_ascii -outDir outputs/snap_010_cropped_test -to NDnet_ascii -smooth 0
netconv snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a.NDnet -outName snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a_ascii -outDir outputs/snap_010_cropped_test -to NDnet_ascii -smooth 0
skelconv snap_010_s3.U.NDskl -outName snap_010_s3.U_ascii -outDir outputs/snap_010_cropped_test -to NDskl_ascii -smooth 0
```

Then run:

```bash
python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py --verbose \
  --delaunay-ndnet outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_ascii.NDnet \
  --walls-ndnet    outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a_ascii.NDnet \
  --filaments-ndskl outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_ascii.NDskl \
  --walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell \
  --scalar-fields field_value log_field_value \
  --output-csv outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/topology_stats.csv
```

That keeps everything in native form; the script will use IDs from the ASCII files and scalars from the Delaunay ASCII, avoiding any smoothing-induced differences.

The “ASCII” files you’re pointing at are native NDnet/NDskl with a compact layout, and our simple parser isn’t matching their ID/value lines (e.g., lines look like `109272463:true_index` and `...:field_value`), so it finds zero IDs and then VTK parsing fails because those aren’t XML.

Rather than fighting the native format, the easiest way to get matching scalars is:
- Re-export VTU/VTP with no smoothing (`netconv -smooth 0`, `skelconv -smooth 0`), so the `field_value/log_field_value` match the Delaunay values.
- Then run `ndtopo_stats.py` on those VTU/VTP files with `--walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell` and `--scalar-fields field_value log_field_value` (add `mass` if desired). The script reads IDs/scalars via VTK and will populate the CSV.

If you prefer sticking to the native NDnet/NDskl, we’d need to rewrite the parser to handle lines like `109272463:true_index` and the way the scalar values are stored; it’s more involved than the current regexes. Given you already have VTK files and VTK imports work, re-exporting unsmoothed VTK and using those is the cleanest path to consistent stats.

I added an option to auto-convert native NDnet/NDskl to unsmoothed VTU/VTP if desired, and fixed the incorrect ASCII parsing on VTK inputs:

- New flag: `--write-vtk` will run `netconv`/`skelconv` with `-smooth 0` to produce `<stem>_nosmooth.vtu/vtp` and then use those.
- VTK parsing is only attempted on `.vtu/.vtp`; `.NDnet/.NDskl` inputs are converted to ASCII or VTU/VTP depending on `--write-vtk`.
- ASCII parsing no longer tries to read VTK files, avoiding XML errors.

To use unsmoothed VTK generated by the script:
```bash
python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py --verbose --write-vtk \
  --delaunay-ndnet outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010.NDnet \
  --walls-ndnet    outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a.NDnet \
  --filaments-ndskl outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U.NDskl \
  --walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell \
  --scalar-fields field_value log_field_value \
  --output-csv outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/topology_stats.csv \
  --netconv-bin /path/to/netconv --skelconv-bin /path/to/skelconv
```

Or, if you already have unsmoothed VTU/VTP, just point the required args at those (no `--write-vtk` needed).

`ndtopo_stats.py` already has the conversion back in place. When you pass `--write-vtk` it will:

- call `netconv ... -smooth 0` on each NDnet to create `<stem>_nosmooth.vtu` (or pick up an existing `.S000` variant),
- call `skelconv ... -smooth 0` on the NDskl to create `<stem>_nosmooth.vtp` (or pick up `.S000`),
- then load those VTK files, match IDs (walls/delaunay via `true_index` by default; filaments via `cell` -> `int(cell)`), and aggregate scalars from the Delaunay mesh.

To rerun with your existing binaries:

```bash
python scripts/ndtopo_stats.py --verbose --write-vtk \
  --delaunay-ndnet outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010.NDnet \
  --walls-ndnet    outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a.NDnet \
  --filaments-ndskl outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U.NDskl \
  --walls-id-field true_index --filaments-id-field cell \
  --scalar-fields field_value log_field_value \
  --netconv-bin /Users/fules/miniforge3/envs/disperse/bin/netconv \
  --skelconv-bin /Users/fules/miniforge3/envs/disperse/bin/skelconv \
  --output-csv outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/topology_stats.csv
```

You should see the `[info] Converting ...` lines, followed by loaded ID counts and a `[done] wrote ...csv` message. If any ID count shows 0, check that the unsmoothed VTU/VTP files exist (including the `.S000` variant) and that `true_index`/`cell` fields are present.

Two things are getting mixed together here:

1) The way you indexed into the arrays in your spot‑check is misaligned. You turn the ID arrays into sets (which scramble order), then go back to a list and use `.index()`. That picks a random position that happens to contain the same ID value, so you’re sampling unrelated rows. Build a mapping from the original arrays instead of going through a set:

```python
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

paths = {
    "delaunay": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu", "true_index"),
    "walls": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a_nosmooth.vtu", "true_index"),
    "filaments": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp", "cell"),
}

def read(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = {k: read(v[0]) for k,v in paths.items()}

dl_ids = np.array(d["delaunay"].PointData[paths["delaunay"][1]], dtype=int)
wl_ids = np.array(d["walls"].PointData[paths["walls"][1]], dtype=int)
fl_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in d["filaments"].PointData[paths["filaments"][1]]], dtype=int)

dl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(dl_ids)}
wl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(wl_ids)}
fl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(fl_ids)}

common = set(dl_map) & set(wl_map) & set(fl_map)
sample = list(common)[:10]

for cid in sample:
    di, wi, fi = dl_map[cid], wl_map[cid], fl_map[cid]
    for field in ("field_value", "log_field_value", "mass"):
        dv = d["delaunay"].PointData[field][di]
        wv = d["walls"].PointData[field][wi] if field in d["walls"].PointData else None
        fv = d["filaments"].PointData[field][fi] if field in d["filaments"].PointData else None
        print(f"ID {cid} {field}: delaunay={dv}, walls={wv}, filaments={fv}")
```

2) Even with correct indexing, walls/filaments will generally differ from Delaunay: their vertices are generated along manifolds/skeletons and the exporter interpolates or re-samples the scalar fields onto those new vertices. Filament VTPs also don’t carry mass at all. That’s why the overlap script always pulls scalars from the Delaunay mesh only and uses IDs just for membership.

So to sanity‑check value equality, fix the indexing bug first. Expect mass to be missing from filaments, and expect walls/filaments field values to differ because they’re interpolated onto different geometry; the Delaunay values are the authoritative ones for aggregation.

That error comes from the membership check. Use `.keys()` instead of testing the `PointData` wrapper directly. Here’s a corrected snippet you can paste:

```bash
python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

paths = {
    "delaunay": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu", "true_index"),
    "walls": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3_manifolds_JE1a_nosmooth.vtu", "true_index"),
    "filaments": ("outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp", "cell"),
}

def read(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = {k: read(v[0]) for k, v in paths.items()}

dl_ids = np.array(d["delaunay"].PointData[paths["delaunay"][1]], dtype=int)
wl_ids = np.array(d["walls"].PointData[paths["walls"][1]], dtype=int)
fl_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in d["filaments"].PointData[paths["filaments"][1]]], dtype=int)

dl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(dl_ids)}
wl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(wl_ids)}
fl_map = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(fl_ids)}

common = set(dl_map) & set(wl_map) & set(fl_map)
sample = list(common)[:10]

for cid in sample:
    di, wi, fi = dl_map[cid], wl_map[cid], fl_map[cid]
    for field in ("field_value", "log_field_value", "mass"):
        w_has = field in d["walls"].PointData.keys()
        f_has = field in d["filaments"].PointData.keys()
        dv = d["delaunay"].PointData[field][di]
        wv = d["walls"].PointData[field][wi] if w_has else None
        fv = d["filaments"].PointData[field][fi] if f_has else None
        print(f"ID {cid} {field}: delaunay={dv}, walls={wv}, filaments={fv}")
PY
```

This avoids the ambiguous truth-value check and will let you inspect matching IDs correctly.

- The filament VTP stores its own scalar arrays. Even when `field_value` happens to match Delaunay, the filament `log_field_value` is in log10, while Delaunay/walls `log_field_value` is natural log. For example `log10(0.600874…)=‑0.221` (filaments) vs `ln(0.600874…)=‑0.509` (Delaunay/walls). You can verify with:
  ```python
  fv = d["filaments"].PointData["field_value"]
  lv = d["filaments"].PointData["log_field_value"]
  import numpy as np
  print(np.max(np.abs(lv - np.log10(fv))))  # should be ~0
  ```
- In many cases the filament `field_value` itself differs because skeleton points are along arcs and their scalars are re-sampled/interpolated by MSE/skelconv; they’re not guaranteed to be the exact vertex values from the Delaunay mesh. Mass isn’t written to the filaments at all.

This is why `ndtopo_stats.py` always pulls scalars from the Delaunay mesh and only uses IDs to decide membership. If you need consistent logs, compute them yourself from the Delaunay `field_value` (e.g., `np.log` or `np.log10`) rather than trusting the filament `log_field_value` array.

The script doesn’t filter to “.0” entries. In the VTP converted from NDskl, the `cell` field is a float that encodes which Delaunay cell the skeleton point comes from; the decimal suffix (.0/.1/.2/.3) is used to distinguish the cell type (min/saddle/etc). Points sampled along arcs get the same integer part as the critical cell they’re tied to, so casting to `int(cell)` keeps them in the same bucket. That’s why the code uses `int(float(cell))` for IDs.

Those interpolated points carry scalar values interpolated along the arc, so their `field_value`/`log_field_value` can differ from the original vertex values. For aggregation we ignore the filament scalars and take scalars from the Delaunay mesh keyed by the integer ID.

### 2026-01-03 05:01:14Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0417)

The CSV mass comes from the Delaunay mesh, not from the filament file. The “filament count” is just `len(filament IDs)`, but the “filament mass” is the sum of `mass` on those IDs that the script can actually match in the Delaunay point data. If some filament IDs don’t exist in the Delaunay universe (e.g., because of smoothed/interpolated skeleton points, or because the `cell` field doesn’t map cleanly back), they drop out of the mass sum, so mass < count.

Quick check to see how many filament IDs match the Delaunay IDs:

```bash
python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

delaunay = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu"
filaments = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp"

def rd(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = rd(delaunay)
f = rd(filaments)

uni_ids = set(np.array(d.PointData["true_index"], dtype=int))
fil_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in f.PointData["cell"]], dtype=int)
fil_set = set(fil_ids)
matched = fil_set & uni_ids
print("filament IDs:", len(fil_set))
print("matched in Delaunay:", len(matched))
print("unmatched:", len(fil_set - uni_ids))
PY
```

If you’re using smoothed VTPs (e.g., `.S020`) many spline points won’t have matching Delaunay IDs; stick to the unsmoothed conversions (`--write-vtk` → `*_nosmooth.vtp`) for best alignment. If the unmatched count is still nonzero, that explains why filament mass is below the filament count.

The integer part of `cell` in an unsmoothed NDskl does correspond to the source cell/critical point ID, and when you convert that NDskl to an unsmoothed VTP (`-smooth 0` or `*_nosmooth.vtp`), those integer IDs should match the `true_index` in the Delaunay mesh.

When filament count ≫ filament mass in the CSV, it means some filament IDs didn’t resolve in the Delaunay universe, so their mass wasn’t added. Typical causes:

- Using a smoothed skeleton (e.g., `.S020`) — spline-resampled points can carry `cell` values that no longer map cleanly back, or the file may drop `cell` altogether.
- Using a VTP that’s been filtered/processed so `cell` got lost or altered.
- Using a Delaunay file where the `true_index` field is missing or was renamed.

To verify, run the quick overlap check I shared (counts of filament IDs vs how many are found in Delaunay). If you see a gap, switch to unsmoothed conversions (`--write-vtk` → `*_nosmooth.vtp/.vtu`), and keep `walls-id-field=true_index`, `filaments-id-field=cell`. If the filament IDs fully match the Delaunay IDs, filament mass should align with count (assuming mass=1 per particle in the Delaunay file).

When filament mass < filament count it means many filament IDs aren’t found in the Delaunay point IDs, so their mass never gets added. With `--write-vtk` the converter makes `_nosmooth` VTP/VTU files and we take IDs from `int(cell)` (filaments) and `true_index` (Delaunay). If those sets don’t overlap fully, mass drops.

Please run this quick check to see how many filament IDs actually match the Delaunay IDs and whether there are negative/odd `cell` values:

```bash
python - <<'PY'
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader, vtkXMLPolyDataReader
from vtkmodules.numpy_interface import dataset_adapter as dsa
import numpy as np

delaunay = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_nosmooth.vtu"
filaments = "outputs/snap_010_cropped_test/snap_010_s3.U_nosmooth.S000.vtp"

def rd(path):
    r = vtkXMLUnstructuredGridReader() if path.endswith(".vtu") else vtkXMLPolyDataReader()
    r.SetFileName(path); r.Update()
    return dsa.WrapDataObject(r.GetOutput())

d = rd(delaunay)
f = rd(filaments)

uni_ids = set(np.array(d.PointData["true_index"], dtype=int))
fil_cells = np.array(f.PointData["cell"])
fil_ids = np.array([int(float(x)) for x in fil_cells], dtype=int)
fil_set = set(fil_ids)

missing = fil_set - uni_ids
print("filament IDs total:", len(fil_set))
print("matched in Delaunay:", len(fil_set & uni_ids))
print("unmatched:", len(missing))
print("cell min/max:", fil_cells.min(), fil_cells.max())
print("negative cell count:", np.sum(fil_cells < 0))
PY
```

- If `unmatched` is large or there are many negative `cell` values, those are the IDs not contributing to mass. Negative/infinity/dummy nodes from the skeleton won’t have a matching Delaunay `true_index`; you can filter them out before aggregation.
- If `matched` still falls short even with unsmoothed VTP, double‑check that the files being read are the `_nosmooth` ones and that Delaunay contains the `true_index` array. If `true_index` is missing, the script will fall back to another field and IDs won’t line up.

Once we see the overlap numbers, we can decide whether to drop negative cells or adjust the ID field to get mass ≈ count.

Most of the filament points simply don’t map back to your Delaunay IDs. The quick check showed ~601k unique filament `cell` IDs but only ~115k of those exist in the Delaunay `true_index` set; the rest are unmatched. That’s why filament mass (taken from Delaunay) is far below the filament count.

Why unmatched? In the VTP, `cell` is a skeleton-side identifier. Only the critical-point samples line up with the original Delaunay vertex IDs; the many interpolated points along arcs carry `cell` values that aren’t present in the Delaunay file (note the max `cell` ≈ 44M vs Delaunay IDs up to ~3.3M). Those points therefore contribute to the filament count but not to mass, because there’s no Delaunay scalar to attach.

To close the gap you’d need an ID field on the filaments that truly matches the Delaunay vertices (e.g., a propagated `true_index`/`source_index` if available), or operate at the critical-point level only. With the current fields, mass can only be summed for the subset of filament points whose IDs exist in the Delaunay mesh.

If the origin/bounds still look like the global domain (e.g., starting at 0,0 instead of the crop’s x0,y0), the resampler is using full-box bounds.

2) Likewise check the flattened density VTI and the PNG camera/center by opening the VTI in ParaView and seeing whether the bounding box matches the crop.

If you see global bounds, the fix is to have `batch_clip.py` resample within the clipped crop bounds rather than the original dataset. In the current script the z-origin is scaled, but x/y bounds are not re-centered per-crop before resampling, so a shifted crop samples the wrong region and the PNGs pick up neighbor tiles. Adjust the resample/clip bounds in `batch_clip.py` to the input data’s bounds (post-crop) before `ResampleToImage`/flattening; use those bounds for the render camera too.

If you want, I can patch `batch_clip.py` to base resampling and rendering bounds on the input dataset bounds (after cropping) so each crop stays local and the artifacts disappear.

### 2026-01-03 08:33:01Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0439)

`analyze_snapshot.py` deliberately appends the format tag (e.g., `_delaunay_vtu.vtu`, `_manifolds_vtu_JE1a.S020.vtu`, `_filaments_U_vtp.S020.vtp`) to the prefix so the filenames are self‑describing and don’t collide when you change formats/tags. It also matches what `netconv`/`skelconv` emit so downstream steps (batch_clip, stats) can find the files reliably. If you removed the explicit extension from the base name, you’d need to adjust the loaders and glob patterns accordingly, otherwise the locating logic will break.

<a id="t-000858"></a>
### 2026-01-03 08:37:10Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0441)

The extra tag isn’t just “format=VTU” – it also encodes what was exported and how, e.g.:

- what it represents: `delaunay_vtu`, `manifolds_vtu_JE1a`, `filaments_U_vtp`
- smoothing iterations: `.S020` (or absence if none)
- arc/manifold tags: `JE1a`, `U`, etc.

The extension alone only tells you the file type; the tag in the stem preserves provenance and prevents collisions when you change tags or smoothing. It also matches what `netconv/skelconv` emit, so downstream scripts (batch_clip, stats) can locate files reliably. Dropping it would require reworking those patterns and would lose that contextual info.

### 2026-01-03 08:41:19Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

The `vtu/vtp` bit in the stem comes from the naming scheme of `netconv/skelconv` and encodes more than “this is a VTU file”:

- It distinguishes what was exported and with which tool/option set: e.g. `delaunay_vtu`, `manifolds_vtu_JE1a`, `filaments_U_vtp`.
- It keeps stems unique when you change tags or smoothing, so a `..._delaunay_vtu.vtu` won’t collide with a future `..._delaunay_vtk.vtk` or a `..._manifolds_vtu_JE1a.vtu`.
- Downstream scripts (batch_clip, stats) look for these stems; removing the tag would break those lookups.

So the extension marks the file type, while the stem tag preserves provenance and avoids collisions; it isn’t purely redundant.

The tiling is coming from the Delaunay export, not the filename. In your run the NDnet reports

```
Bounding box: x0=[500,500,100],
              delta=[1000,1000,200].
```

but the crop you asked for is only 500 Mpc/h wide in x and y. Because `delaunay_3D` was run with periodic boundaries, it keeps the full 1000 Mpc/h domain size and wraps guard particles across the box, so when you visualize the VTU you see a second copy offset by one box length in X/Y.

To keep the bounds local to the crop (and avoid the repeated footprint):

- Disable periodic wrapping for subboxes: run `analyze_snapshot.py` with `--periodic false` and `--delaunay-btype natural` (or at least `--delaunay-btype natural`). That will set the Delaunay NDnet delta to the crop size and stop the wraparound.
- If you’re using `batch_crop_and_clip.py`, add `--delaunay-btype natural --periodic false` (or edit the defaults) so each tile is treated as a non‑periodic box.

After rerunning with natural boundaries, the Delaunay VTU should have bounds matching the crop and the density images should stop showing the repeated tile.

```bash

  --periodic false --delaunay-btype natural
```

After rerunning with natural boundaries, the Delaunay NDnet/VTU bounds should match the crop size and the density images should stop showing the repeated tile. If you want me to bake those boundary settings into the batch driver as the default, I can do that next.

### 2026-01-03 20:41:21Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0455)

The core issue is that we’re still telling `delaunay_3D` to run periodic on a box that doesn’t start at the origin. Periodic mode assumes a domain from 0 to L; when you pass a cropped NDfield with min=(500,500,100) and still use `-periodic`, DisPerSE wraps guard particles as if the box started at 0 and had size 1,000 Mpc/h. The NDnet log shows that: `x0=[500,500,100], delta=[1000,1000,200]` — it has effectively grown your 500 Mpc/h crop to a 1,000 Mpc/h periodic box, which is why you see a repeated footprint in X/Y (and Z if the delta is larger than the crop).

By contrast, the cropping logic in `analyze_snapshot.py` is fine: we write the NDfield header with the crop min/max, and the particle count matches the crop. It’s the periodic tessellation on a shifted box that’s causing the duplication.

To avoid the repeats for tiles that don’t start at 0:

- Run crops with non‑periodic boundaries: `--periodic false --delaunay-btype natural` (or skip `--periodic` and set `--delaunay-btype natural`). This keeps the tessellation confined to the crop bounds.
- If using `batch_crop_and_clip.py`, add those flags (or change defaults) so each crop is treated as a standalone non‑periodic box.

If you want to keep periodicity, you’d need to rebase coordinates so each crop starts at 0 and adjust the NDfield header accordingly, but the simpler fix is to treat cropped tiles as non‑periodic.

### 2026-01-03 20:44:59Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

To keep periodicity without tiling artifacts, the clean approach is to rebase each crop so its min corner is at (0,0,0), run the periodic Delaunay/MSE on that rebased catalog, and then shift the resulting VTU/NDnet/NDskl back to the original coordinates. That way periodic wrapping occurs within the 0→(dx,dy,dz) box instead of the global 1 Gpc frame. Key steps:

1) When writing the NDfield for a crop, subtract the crop origin from the coordinates and set the header BBOX to `[0 0 0] [dx dy dz]` in the chosen units.
2) Run `delaunay_3D` and `mse` with `-periodic` on this rebased catalog.
3) Before exporting VTU/VTP (netconv/skelconv), add the crop origin back to the point coordinates so downstream files sit in the global frame.
   - netconv/skelconv don’t shift coordinates themselves, so we’d need a post-step (e.g., a Transform in Paraview/Python) that adds the origin to the output datasets.
4) All file naming can stay the same; only the coordinate frames change.

Cropping after Delaunay would still leave wrapped cells in the tessellation; shifting avoids introducing the extra periodic images in the first place.

If you want, I can implement this shift/unshift inside `analyze_snapshot.py`: rebase the NDfield coordinates and bbox to the crop origin, run periodic tessellation/MSE, then add the origin offset back to the exported VTU/VTP outputs. Let me know and I’ll patch it.

Translating the VTK exports is straightforward (we can read, add the crop origin to points, and write back), but doing the same to the native DisPerSE files would require a format-aware rewriter.

If you’re OK with a staged fix, I can:
- Rebase the NDfield to the crop origin before Delaunay/MSE (keeps periodic tessellation local).
- After netconv/skelconv, translate all VTK outputs (VTU/VTP/VTI) by the crop origin so they sit in global coordinates.
- Leave the NDnet/NDskl binaries in the rebased frame (they’ll still align with the translated VTKs).

If you need NDnet/NDskl shifted too, we’d need to either:
- Convert them to VTK, shift, and rely on those shifted VTKs for downstream use, or
- Write a dedicated converter that understands the NDnet/NDskl binary layout to apply an offset.

Let me know which approach you prefer, and I’ll implement the translation for the VTK outputs right away, or we can explore a deeper converter for the native files.

What I proposed earlier is exactly the “first stage” I mentioned: rebase the NDfield to the crop origin, run periodic tessellation/MSE, and then add the crop origin back only when writing the VTK outputs. In that setup the native NDnet/NDskl stay in the rebased frame (coordinates start at 0 for each crop), while the VTU/VTP/VTI files are shifted back to global so they line up in ParaView. “They’ll still align with the translated VTKs” means: all the VTK exports sit in global space together, but the raw NDnet/NDskl don’t—they’re still local.

Getting NDnet/NDskl themselves into global coordinates is the hard part, because they’re binary and don’t have a simple “offset” knob; we’d need a format-aware rewriter. A safe, workable path is:

- Rebase NDfield to the crop origin; run periodic Delaunay/MSE.
- Shift all exported VTKs (Delaunay, manifolds, filaments) by the crop origin so they’re in global coordinates.
- If you need the NDnet/NDskl in global space too, convert them to VTK, apply the same shift, and use those shifted VTKs for downstream steps.

If you want me to implement the rebase + VTK shift in `analyze_snapshot.py` now (leaving the native NDnet/NDskl rebased), I can do that. If you really need the native NDnet/NDskl shifted as well, we’ll need a custom converter to edit those binaries safely. Let me know which route you prefer.

Here’s a quick refactor/streamlining pass on the key scripts (no code changes made, just findings and suggestions):

**analyze_snapshot.py**
- Coordinate rebasing/shift-back is now split across NDfield writing and VTK export. Consider encapsulating the “rebase → run → shift-back” logic into a small helper or a dataclass that carries `crop_min_scaled`, to avoid scattering that state.
- Filename handling: after we simplified stems, there are multiple glob/rename paths. Centralize naming in one helper (e.g., `make_delaunay_name`, `make_manifold_name`, `make_skeleton_name`) so downstream scripts don’t need to guess stems or smoothing suffixes.
- VTK shift depends on optional vtkmodules; if missing, we log and skip. If that’s critical, add a single guard early (e.g., warn once if shift will be skipped), instead of per-file checks.
- Summary stats: `summarize_vtk`/`write_stats_csv` are embedded here and also in other scripts. Consider factoring them into a tiny utility module shared across scripts to avoid duplication.
- CLI: some options are deprecated/flagged in the guide (“don’t use blocks”), but still present. If they’re truly unused, hide or default them appropriately to reduce surface area.

**batch_clip.py**
- Repetition in render/save: `render_png`/`render_composite_png` have similar setup. Could reduce duplication by a small renderer factory and a shared “color by” helper.
- Bounds/resampling: after the recent fix, density uses clipped bounds; ensure the same pattern for any future additions (e.g., if walls/filaments ever get resampled).
- Stats writer duplicates code from analyze_snapshot; could reuse a shared utility.
- Command-line parsing is flat; grouping PNG options vs core options could improve readability/help output.

**batch_crop_and_clip.py**
- Filename discovery: now globbing for manifolds/skeletons. Wrap that logic in a helper (`find_manifolds`, `find_skeleton`) to avoid repeating patterns and make errors clearer.
- Command construction is verbose. A small builder for analyze/clip commands (returning lists) would make it easier to maintain and to tweak defaults (e.g., periodic/natural).
- Unit handling: we now rebase/shift in analyze; ensure the batch driver’s unit assumptions are documented and maybe logged per crop to aid debugging.
- Stats step is unconditional; if that should be optional, a flag would help (but keep default on).

**ndtopo_stats.py**
- Narrow focus is good; could add a short sanity check/report on how many IDs matched vs unmatched (you already do verbose logging; making that always-on in non-verbose mode could help users interpret mass < count).
- The `--write-vtk` conversion path assumes `netconv/skelconv`; a brief warning if those aren’t found (instead of fatal) might make it friendlier.

If you want, I can implement any of these refactors (e.g., central naming helpers and a shared stats utility) to reduce duplication and make behavior more consistent.

### 2026-01-04 01:40:09Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0542)

To have a Quarto doc emit both HTML and PDF:

1) In your QMD front‑matter, list both formats:
```yaml
---
title: "My Report"
format:
  html: default
  pdf:
    documentclass: article   # optional
    toc: true                # optional extras
---
```

2) Ensure PDF tooling is available:
   - Install Quarto (if not already): e.g., `brew install quarto`.
   - Install a LaTeX engine: simplest is `quarto install tinytex` (or full TeX Live/MacTeX).

3) Render both at once:
   - `quarto render myfile.qmd`  # will produce HTML and PDF because both are listed.
   - Or, explicitly: `quarto render myfile.qmd --to html,pdf`.

If LaTeX is missing, PDF will fail—install tinytex via Quarto and rerun.

- This prevents the skip and lets stats and slab steps run even when the arc tag is missing in the filename.

### 2026-01-04 07:13:54Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0548)

`ckup` came from DisPerSE’s own naming, not from our script. When `mse` saves the Morse–Smale complex with simplification (e.g., `-nsig 5`), it also writes a backup skeleton as `…_s5.MSC.backup.NDskl`. That file has no arc tag (`U`) in the name, so you see `…_s5.ckup.NDskl` alongside the expected manifolds file. It didn’t replace `U`; it was just the only NDskl the batch script could see because its tag search was too strict. I loosened the search so it will use the newest NDskl even if the tag is missing.

In earlier tiles you were getting the expected tagged skeleton (e.g. `<prefix>_s5.U.NDskl`), so the batch script found it and kept going. Midway through, `mse` emitted only the backup skeleton name (`<prefix>_s5.MSC.backup.NDskl`) for that crop—DisPerSE writes that backup after simplification and, in this case, never produced a tagged `..._U.NDskl`. Because the batch script was only looking for filenames that contained the arc tag (`U`), it couldn’t find this backup-only NDskl, so stats and slab steps were skipped starting with the first crop that had only the backup file. We’ve now loosened the glob to fall back to any NDskl (including the backup name), so the issue won’t recur, and you can rerun to generate the missing outputs.

I traced the root cause: DisPerSE sometimes only writes a “backup” skeleton (`..._sX.MSC.backup.NDskl`) without the arc tag `U` in the filename. Our batch logic was only looking for tagged names, so those crops got skipped.

Fix applied:
- In `scripts/analyze_snapshot.py`, `locate_dump_arcs_file` now detects when the newest NDskl is missing the tag and creates a tagged alias (`<prefix>_U.NDskl`) via hardlink (or copy if hardlink not possible). Downstream steps will therefore see a proper `U`-tagged file even if DisPerSE only emitted the backup name.

To regenerate missing stats/slabs:
- Rerun the affected crops (or the whole batch). The rerun will create the tagged alias and downstream steps will proceed using the `U`-tagged file.

If you prefer, I can also add an explicit warning whenever a backup-only name is encountered, but the current change already ensures a `U`-named file is present.

### 2026-01-04 07:20:28Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0554)

Understood—you want the root cause, not just an alias. A few likely reasons MSE emitted only the “backup” skeleton instead of the tagged `U` file, plus what to check:

1) Persistence/cancellation can delete the requested arcs
   - If `-nsig 5` is very aggressive, the simplification pass can cancel all arcs of a given tag, so no `U` skeleton is written and only the MSC backup remains.
   - Check the MSE log for “Cancelling pairs …” and how many arcs remain. If zero `U` arcs survive, there’s nothing to write.

2) Output tag not actually requested
   - Ensure `-dumpArcs U` was present in the command for those crops. If a run was restarted without `U`, only the manifolds and backup MSC would exist.

3) Reused prefix colliding with older outputs
   - If a previous run with the same prefix produced a backup but no `U`, and a later run failed/was killed before writing `U`, the “newest” file could be the old backup. Clean the crop folder and rerun to be sure you’re seeing a fresh MSE output.

4) Disk/kill during write
   - A killed MSE (e.g., OOM, SIGKILL) might leave only intermediate/backup files. In your logs, verify MSE completed the skeleton dump (“Saving 3D skeleton to file … done.”).

How to investigate and resolve:
- For an affected crop, rerun just MSE manually with verbose logs:
  ```
  mse <crop_prefix>.NDnet -outName <prefix> -outDir <dir> -nsig 5 -dumpArcs U -dumpManifolds JE1a
  ```
  Check the console: look for “Dumping skeleton … done.” and count of arcs.
- Lower persistence temporarily (e.g., `-nsig 3` or add `-cut` thresholds) to see if `U` is emitted; if so, the `-nsig 5` setting is pruning everything.
- Ensure the crop directory is empty before rerunning, so stale backups aren’t picked up.
- Confirm the batch command actually includes `--dump-arcs U` for all tiles.
- If MSE logs show arcs are present but the `U` file isn’t written, capture that log snippet; it could be a DisPerSE bug in that build.

Once you confirm arcs are being produced and written, the `U` file should reappear and downstream steps can use it without relying on aliases.

### 2026-01-04 07:54:53Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0556)

`mse` writes two skeletons: the final one for the arc tag you requested (e.g. `_s5.U.NDskl`) and a backup of the unsimplified complex before cancellations. That backup uses an internal tag, and in your build it shows up as `_s5.C.backup.NDskl` (earlier runs showed `_s5.MSC.backup.NDskl`). The “C” is DisPerSE’s own label for that pre-simplification/complete skeleton, not something the scripts are adding. When no `_s5.U.NDskl` is present but a `_s5.C.backup.NDskl` is, it usually means:

- All `U` arcs were cancelled by the chosen persistence (`-nsig 5`) so no tagged skeleton was emitted, leaving only the backup, or
- The run was interrupted or reused a directory with stale backup files and never wrote a fresh `_s5.U.NDskl`.

How to get the proper `_s5.U.NDskl`:
1) Rerun `mse` for that crop in a clean (or emptied) crop folder with `-dumpArcs U -nsig 5` and watch the log: you should see arc counts and “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl … done.” If the log shows zero `U` arcs remaining, lower `-nsig` or adjust cuts so arcs survive.
2) Ensure every batch call includes `--dump-arcs U`.
3) Avoid reusing old crop directories when debugging—old backups can be picked up as “newest” if a run fails before writing `U`.

Once `mse` actually produces `_s5.U.NDskl`, downstream steps will prefer that file and ignore the backup.

Unlikely it’s a filename-length issue. APFS/HFS allow ~255‑byte filenames and ~1K paths; your example name is ~80 chars, well under the limits. DisPerSE chooses the stem: when it writes the “backup” skeleton (unsimplified complex), it uses its own tag in the name—older runs showed `_MSC.backup`, your build is emitting `_C.backup`. That tag comes from MSE, not from truncation.

If you want to be sure, check the MSE log for that crop: it will print the exact “Saving 3D skeleton to file …” line. If it only prints the backup and not `_s5.U.NDskl`, the issue is that the tagged skeleton wasn’t written (e.g., arcs pruned/cancelled or the run interrupted), not that the name got mangled by length.

When MSE writes the unsimplified/backup skeleton it inserts an internal tag before `.backup` (you’ve seen `_s5.MSC.backup.NDskl` earlier; in your recent runs it’s `_s5.C.backup.NDskl`). That token is chosen by MSE and can vary by build or by which internal complex it decides to stash—nothing in our code is renaming or truncating it, and the filenames are far below any filesystem length limits.

### 2026-01-04 08:12:58Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0562)

Those filenames come straight from MSE; our scripts don’t rewrite them. MSE builds its output name as:

```
<outName>_s<sigma>.<tag>.NDskl
```

- For sigma it prints a float, so `-nsig 5` becomes `s5.00000`.
- `<outName>` is whatever prefix we pass (your long crop name ending in `_z900000-1000000`), so that substring naturally appears in every file.
- The extra `_z900000-1000000` you see after `s5.00000` is not a truncation artifact; it’s still part of the original prefix being repeated in the composed name. MSE isn’t changing it because of length—it’s just concatenating prefix + sigma tag + “backup”.

Why no `_U.NDskl` then?
- If MSE cancels all `U` arcs at `nsig=5`, it won’t write a tagged `U` skeleton and you’ll only see the backup. The MSE log will show arc counts and whether it wrote “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl”.
- If a run was interrupted or a directory reused, you can end up with only the backup file from a prior run.

How to verify/fix on a crop:
1) Clean that crop folder (or move files aside) and rerun just MSE with a shorter `--output-prefix` as a test:
   ```
   mse <crop>.NDnet -outName test -outDir <crop_dir> -nsig 5 -dumpArcs U -dumpManifolds JE1a
   ```
   Watch the console for “Saving 3D skeleton to file …U.NDskl” and the arc counts.
2) If the log shows zero `U` arcs at `nsig=5`, lower `-nsig` or adjust `-cut` until arcs survive, then rerun.
3) If the log shows arcs and “Saving …U.NDskl” but the file is missing, let me know—that would indicate an MSE bug rather than naming/length.

So the odd-looking `_s5.00000_…backup` name is MSE’s normal composition (prefix + sigma tag + “backup”), not a path-length distortion; the real issue is that a `U` skeleton wasn’t written for that run.

I see why the batch failed: `ndtopo_stats.py` looked for the unsmoothed filament VTP as `_S000.vtp`, but `skelconv -smooth 0` emitted `..._S000.S000.vtp`. I’ve updated `scripts/ndtopo_stats.py` to accept that extra `.S000` variant when converting NDskl to VTP, so the stats step won’t error.

Changes made:
- `scripts/ndtopo_stats.py`: `ensure_vtp_from_ndskl` now also checks for a `*.S000.vtp` sibling in addition to `*_S000.vtp`.

You can rerun the failed crop; the stats step should now succeed and the slab processing will continue.

### 2026-01-04 08:40:45Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0568)

I cleaned up the naming to avoid double `S000` on filament VTPs:

- `ndtopo_stats.py` now strips any existing smoothing tag and, for skelconv, does **not** pre-append `_S000`—since skelconv adds `.S000` itself when `-smooth 0` is used. It looks for `foo.vtp`, `foo_S000.vtp`, or `foo.S000.vtp` after conversion.
- Netconv unsmoothed VTU still uses a single `_S000` suffix.

Re-run the batch; the filament VTP should come out with only one `S000` and the stats step won’t fail on a missing file.

<a id="t-000986"></a>
### 2026-01-04 08:53:08Z — user — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0569)

does the ndtopo_stat.py script test for the existinece of S000 files before it generates them?

<a id="t-000987"></a>
### 2026-01-04 08:53:16Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0570)

Yes. In `ndtopo_stats.py`, both converters check for an existing unsmoothed file before running `netconv`/`skelconv`:

- For NDnet → VTU: it strips any existing smoothing tag and looks for `<stem>_S000.vtu`. If found, it uses it; otherwise it runs `netconv … -smooth 0` to create it.
- For NDskl → VTP: it strips any smoothing tag and looks for `foo.vtp`, `foo_S000.vtp`, or `foo.S000.vtp`. If any exist, it uses the existing one; only if none are present does it call `skelconv … -smooth 0` to generate it.

So it will reuse existing `_S000` outputs and only generate them when missing.

The key failure is `Error code "No space left on device"` from the VTK writers—that corrupted the partially written VTK/PNG files, leading to downstream read errors (`offsets array is not long enough`, `File not readable`). This wasn’t caused by the code logic; it’s a disk/full-quota issue.

How to recover:
1) Free space (disk/quota) where `outputs/` lives. Check `df -h` or your quota.
2) Delete the incomplete slab folder so it can be regenerated cleanly:
   ```
   rm -rf outputs/quijote_batches/crop_x0-500_y500-1000_z700-800/slab_z700
   ```
3) Re-run just that slab (or rerun the batch for that crop once space is available).

After space is freed, the “offsets not long enough” and PNG write errors will disappear because the writers will complete successfully. If you want, I can add a guard to skip PNGs/reads when a write fails, but the root cause here is insufficient disk space.

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0585)

They’re two exports of the same Delaunay NDnet at different points in the workflow:

- `crop_x500-1000_y500-1000_z0-100_delaunay.vtu` — written by `analyze_snapshot.py` via `netconv` using whatever smoothing you requested there (e.g., `--delaunay-smooth 20` → `_S020`; if you left smoothing at 0, it may have no tag). It’s the “official” Delaunay mesh you asked to export.

- `crop_x500-1000_y500-1000_z0-100_delaunay_S000.vtu` — written later by `ndtopo_stats.py` when you pass `--write-vtk`. That script converts the native NDnet to an unsmoothed VTU with a fixed `_S000` suffix for stats matching. It ignores any prior smoothing and forces `-smooth 0`.

So: the `_S000` file is the unsmoothed, stats-only copy generated on demand by `ndtopo_stats.py`; the plain `delaunay.vtu` is the one produced during the main analysis with your chosen smoothing settings.

### 2026-01-04 18:42:22Z — assistant — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`

Session: [2025-12-28 15:07:54 — `019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342`](2025-12-28__15-07-54__019b67a5-bfb8-7bc2-9dab-29d5821a6342.md#m-0587)

They’re two separate exports of the same NDnet:

- `..._delaunay.vtu` was written by `analyze_snapshot.py` during the main run. It uses your requested Delaunay smoothing (default 0 if you didn’t set `--delaunay-smooth`) and is shifted back to global coordinates.
- `..._delaunay_S000.vtu` was written later by `ndtopo_stats.py` when you used `--write-vtk`. That conversion forces `-smooth 0` and uses the rebased NDnet directly (no global shift).

So even with smoothing=0 they differ: one is global-shifted (and possibly smoothed), the other is unsmoothed in the rebased crop frame. The size difference comes from re-running `netconv` with a different output stem; if you want to avoid the extra file, point `ndtopo_stats.py` at the existing `..._delaunay.vtu` (use `--delaunay-vtk` instead of `--delaunay-ndnet`), or drop `--write-vtk`.
